The page offers a strange kind of invitation. Not a blank stare, but a soft, shimmering potential, as if the sentences have been sieved out of the air and landed in little, expectant piles. I suppose you could say that every time I sit down to write something, I’m holding my breath for the first word. But today the prompt is simple and terrifying: “You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.”

Whatever comes to me might include a waltz through memory, a stuttering puzzle of jokes, a sudden seriousness about the weight of things. Perhaps it will settle in unexpected corners—like the time I spent in my grandmother's kitchen when the kettle refused to whistle. The silence in that room was dense, textured with the low hum of refrigerator motors and the quiet clatter of old ceramic mugs stacking themselves in my imagination. I remember thinking that silence was just unspoken noise, waiting for the right word to coax it out.

Maybe that feeling is familiar to you too. You sit with a thousand words, a limit that is both generous and exacting. It feels like being given a long road with a sign saying “go anywhere,” while the guardrail whispers, “only this much.” I could go anywhere, but the “whatever comes to me” is the real compass. What comes to me now is a vision of walking through a city I’ve never seen in reality but have visited countless times in dreams. Neon signs flicker in alphabets that translate themselves as I pass—some meanings obvious, others carrying the delicious charge of mystery.

The city is alive, but not in the manic pace of headlines. It’s alive in the weight of ordinary moments—an old man playing chess on a stoop, a dog whose tail wags to a rhythm no one else can hear, a child releasing a balloon and the abrupt, tender sadness of seeing a bright color float against the pale blue like a promise getting lost. I imagine the balloon drifting toward a skyline that glows faintly, the way dusk settles over rooftops in a film shot on that edge between gold and indigo.

Thoughts like these invite me to consider how often we overlook the small stories that shape us. There’s a bird outside now, a crow I think, who demands attention with its hacking caw. It sounds almost conversational—an urgent, inquisitive, maybe even judgmental “Hey, you. Come out.” I’ve never heard a crow say something specific, but I imagine they are quite opinionated. Perhaps this one is tired of digital noise and wants to reconnect the world. Or maybe it’s just hungry.

The whatever that comes next is connected to a kitchen scene I keep revisiting. A large pot of soup steams, carrying aromas of cilantro and garlic, the kind that make your nose remember how to breathe. There’s also the matter of a broken watch, a childhood relic from a grandfather who wore it with a stubborn pride even though it stopped at 7:12 long before I was born. I still possess it because it was the only thing that fit his hands in my imagination. When I pick up the watch, I’m reminded that time is not a precise measurement but a collage of ticks, long pauses, and sometimes an entire afternoon spent staring out a rainy window while the kettle boils on autopilot.

“Whatever comes to me,” you see, often carries the weight of connection. The connections might be with people, or with the objects that remind us of them. There are memories coded into the lining of a coat, a smell that instantly propels me into a different era, a song that wraps around my ribs as if it were a physical thing and squeezes.

It’s strange to think about how the mind is always traveling. Right now I’m moving through these sentences, but somewhere beneath, the subconscious is wandering down a trail where my earliest friendship resides—playing tag until the sun melted into its pillow, voting on which dinosaur was the fiercest, trading snacks for little, shiny favors made from folding paper. There’s a certain nostalgia for those uncomplicated trades; the currency was something that won't appear on any balance sheet, but it was rich in a way that now feels rare.

There’s also the current moment, which is as vivid as a rash decision in a crowded room. I’m listening to the low hum of a fan, the thin squeak of a chair, the distant murmur of yet another evening settling. Outside, a plane draws a white line across a sky that is softer than blue—maybe the color belongs to a painting, or to that moment right before sleep where the mind is still gliding above consciousness. I like to think about what happens in between sentences, those tiny spaces that usually go unnoticed. It’s there where a thought is born, then scoots to the edge and waits for its cue.

The prompt may have been “whatever comes to you,” but I realize now that it also means “Whatever you bring to it matters.” Listening for the whisper is an act of responsibility. I could produce nonsense, or I could follow the current of my most curious observations. So here’s another: sometimes, in the middle of a task, the world pauses and allows me a moment to look out of a literal or figurative window. Today, the window shows the cityscape described before, but also it’s a small square of light in a living room, filtered through venetian blinds. Stripes of brightness fall across a table, highlighting the grooves of old wood. The light shifts, slow and forgiving, the way a friend might shift in their seat to make you comfortable.

I might also mention the uncanny ability our minds have to jump from one theme to another without an obvious bridge. It happened earlier, right when I thought of the crow, that the idea of “communication” bristled. Maybe the crow was part of the conversation—its caw a punctuation mark—maybe not. It was the sudden sense that in the world of words, the birds, the steam, the broken watch, and the balloon could all be characters in the same scene. In that way, writing is a little like trying to conduct a parade where each float is a different thought. I have to give them room to march, but also keep them within the path.

Let’s take a small detour. There’s a hill I remember from a late summer afternoon. I can picture the long grass brushing against my wrists, the wind gentle enough to carry the scent of damp earth and the far-away buzz of cicadas. Up that hill, a small sign stood, weathered and leaning. All it said was “Pause.” No instructions beyond the word, just a stillness that invited reflection. That feeling is what I’m trying to catch now. The “whatever” is the pause. It is the breath between sentences where I choose the next direction.

As I near the final stretch of these 1000 words, I think of what might come after them. Perhaps it will be a continuation, or perhaps the silence will fall for a moment like a curtain lifting. But there is no finality here, only a lingering note—an open invitation to keep going. Maybe the best thing about “write whatever comes to you” is not the words themselves but the reminder that the human mind tends to wander to places that are alive with meaning, places both big and small. A floating balloon, a quiet crow, a summer hill—they all live inside us, whispering that every day is a mosaic of moments, and that the art of writing is simply choosing which shards to lift into the light.

The room is easing into evening now, and I can hear more of the city outside doing precisely the same. Someone laughs two rooms down, and the sound rolls toward me as if it were a wave. The radiator clicks, the fan hums, and the soft whistle of the kettle finally releases its steam. Maybe some future me will look back at these words and remember the exact day the crow demanded attention. Or maybe future me will have forgotten the crow entirely and instead focus on the way these sentences tried to capture the feeling of standing on a hill, of watching a balloon drift, of listening for a pause.

However the future looks, I am content that the “whatever” always lands somewhere worth listening to. And so I will end with this: may you find your own whatever. Let it come soft or loud, logical or wildly disjointed. Thank the absurdities. Follow the quiet cues. Write.
